Learning Objectives
Identify malignancies that metastasize to the upper extremity.

Of patients with metastatic disease in bone, 20% have upper extremity involvement.
Most common site is the humerus (>50%)

Upper extremity function is integral to activities of daily living, including the following:
Bathing, dressing, toileting, and eating
Use of an assistive device (especially with concomitant lower extremity disease).
Obtaining radiographs of the upper extremities is prudent in patients with confirmed lower
extremity metastatic disease.
Protection of the upper extremities from weight bearing is easier than that of the lower
extremities.
The most common primary carcinomas metastasizing to the upper extremities include
prostate, breast, lung, thyroid, and renal carcinomas.
Lung and renal cell carcinomas have a predilection for bones in the forearm and hand (acral
metastases).

Introduction
Metastatic bone disease is the most common destructive bone pathology encountered
by all orthopaedic surgeons. In 2017, the American Cancer Society estimated there were
1.7 million new cancer diagnoses, with approximately 50% developing bone
metastases.1 Approximately 20% of all osseous metastases occur in the upper extremity,
with more than 50% occurring in the humerus, making the humerus the second most
commonly involved long bone. The humerus accounts for 16% to 39% of all impending
or completed pathologic fractures in long bones.2,3 Similar to their lower extremity
counterparts, upper extremity metastatic lesions may cause substantial pain and
functional deficits that may limit activities of daily living and, therefore, overall
independence.
Surgical Indications
Primary goals of surgical management
Relief of pain
Improvement in function
Restoration of skeletal stability

Preoperative Approach
A multidisciplinary approach, involving medical oncology, radiation oncology, orthopaedic
oncology, and musculoskeletal radiology, often is required in the treatment of these patients.
The role of the orthopaedic surgeon must be aligned with the patient’s goals and the
treatment goals set forth by the patient’s primary oncology team.
This requires close communication with the oncology team, especially with respect to timing
of systemic treatment and medical optimization before elective management of any
metastatic lesions.
Most hormone and immunotherapies can be continued during the perioperative period.
Cytotoxic chemotherapy should be withheld because it may inhibit the immune system and
predispose patients to infection or delayed wound healing.
Certain targeted therapies, such as vascular endothelial growth factor receptor tyrosine
kinase inhibitors, considerably delay wound healing and should be withheld until the
surgical wound is completely healed.
Anti–vascular endothelial growth factor medications are prescribed for patients with
thyroid or renal cell carcinoma.
In patients without an established history of malignancy, a biopsy and appropriate staging
must be performed to objectively establish the presence of metastatic disease.
Preoperative Planning
Preoperative considerations
Patient selection (ie, functional status, activity level, comorbidities)
Terminally ill patients (anticipated survival <3 to 6 weeks) may be poor surgical candidates,
necessitating consideration of the benefit of surgical treatmetn.4
No absolute criteria are available to predict survival in patients with metastatic disease of
bone; however, predictive models exist. Important negative prognostic criteria include the
following:
Hypercalcemia
Substantial cytopenia from bone marrow failure
Cachexia
Poor performance status
With current systemic treatment options, patients are living longer, requiring more durable
fixation methods than those used in the past.

Patients with a new diagnosis of bone metastases and who have not yet received treatment
generally have an improved prognosis compared with those who are progressing despite
prior treatment.
Preoperative imaging studies
Preoperative imaging is instrumental.
The entire bone should be visualized, with radiographs obtained in two orthogonal planes.
This aid in assessment for additional lesions away from the site of primary disease.
CT and MRI generally are not needed for preoperative planning unless plain radiographs
are equivocal.
In patients undergoing proximal humerus reconstruction, MRI can be performed to
assess for soft-tissue involvement and the integrity of the rotator cuff in planning the
appropriate implant for reconstruction.
Stability/durability of planned construct
The goal of surgical management is to attain rigid and durable internal fixation and/or
endoprosthetic reconstruction with immediate postoperative use of the upper extremity.
Preoperative embolization
Certain lesions are hypervascular (eg, renal and thyroid metastases)
These lesions can be embolized preoperatively via coiling, cryoablation, or chemical
embolization, especially if an intralesional procedure is planned (Figure 1).

Tourniquets offer an alternative to embolization and afford good hemostasis for lesions
distal enough in the extremity to allow for their use.
Adjunct use of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) bone cement or bone substitutes
These may help fill skeletal voids after curettage of the metastatic lesion and enhance
construct stability as necessary.
Stabilization technique
Skeletal stabilization with intramedullary device (ie, intramedullary nail)
Skeletal stabilization with extramedullary device (ie, plate/screw construct)
Stabilization in metaphyseal or articular lesions may involve the use of an endoprosthetic
implant (eg, hemiarthroplasty, reverse total shoulder arthroplasty [TSA], or total elbow
arthroplasty) in the upper extremity.
Lesion resection (ie, metastasectomy) and reconstruction with the use of a megaprosthesis
or an intercalary implant

Preoperative Planning
The surgical approach to metastatic lesions of the skeleton should allow for
consideration of multiple factors, including the primary cancer type and its associated
characteristics, overall burden of metastatic disease, patient prognosis, anatomic
location, patient expectations, and functional capacity of the patient.1 A multidisciplinary
team approach often is recommended to determine appropriate surgical candidates and
allow for preoperative medical optimization. Specific preoperative considerations include
the timing and cessation of chemotherapeutic and immunotherapy drugs, which may
potentiate perioperative bleeding and postoperative wound healing complications.5 In
addition, the surgical management of all metastatic lesions, regardless of location,
should involve proper consideration of the altered biology of the pathologic bone and its
potential for fracture healing. In general, fracture healing is compromised in pathologic
bone. The degree of healing potential may depend on the underlying histology of the
tumor.
In general, prophylactic stabilization of an impending fracture is preferred over
postfracture fixation, with the former being associated with shorter hospital length of
stays, lower 30-day risk of major medical complications, increased likelihood of
discharge to home, and substantial healthcare cost savings.6,7 The main goal of surgical
management is to provide a construct that allows for immediate stability and
unrestricted activity and that will exceed the patient’s expected longevity without
depending on fracture or defect healing, while also minimizing complications.1 In most
patients, diaphyseal lesions of the upper extremity can be managed via intramedullary
fixation, whereas metaphyseal or periarticular lesions that do not involve the joint can
be managed via cementation and periarticular locking plates.8 The addition of PMMA
cement may be useful in areas in which bone lysis are large or if the anticipated
response to systemic and/or localized therapies is low. The addition of PMMA cement
may improve immediate stability and enhance the durability of the construct.9,10 With
severe bone destruction or if metastasectomy may offer a survival benefit, segmental
resection and reconstruction, which provides the patient with a single, definitive
treatment option, may be considered.11-13 If destruction or risk of failure of the articular
surface exists in patients with periarticular or metaphyseal metastatic disease,

management of pathologic fracture.

Proximal humerus
Complete or impending fractures of the humeral head or anatomic neck usually are
managed with the use of a proximal humerus endoprosthesis.
Intramedullary nails generally are difficult to use in this region because rigid proximal
fixation often cannot be achieved.
Curettage with or without packing with or without plate fixation (Figure 5)
Small proximal humerus lesions that occupy less than 50% of bone stock and preserve
the articular surface
Curettage of the lesion and PMMA bone cement packing may be sufficient for smaller
lesions. Adjunct plate/screw fixation also can be used to confer enhanced stability.
The decision to add internal fixation generally is based on the amount of bone loss and
the structural stability of the bone after curettage.

Standard prosthesis (humeral hemiarthroplasty; Figure 6)
Can be used if the greater and lesser tuberosities are intact.
Cementation is preferred because, classically, ingrowth potential is diminished because

radiation therapy.
A long stemmed implant is preferred, especially if distal lesions are present.
Always plan the location at which the distal stem will terminate based on

If glenoid sided lesions also are present, TSA versus reverse TSA may be considered
based on the integrity of the rotator cuff.15-17
A potential contraindication to reverse TSA is lack of a functioning deltoid muscle (eg,
axillary nerve palsy).

Functional outcomes generally are not as favorable as those with standard
hemiarthroplasty or TSA, partially because of the following:
Soft-tissue attachments often are lost and need to be repaired to the implant.
Glenohumeral instability often may be present because of loss of the soft-tissue
attachments.
Reverse total shoulder endoprostheses offer improved function and decreased rates of
instability compared with standard hemiarthroplasty endoprostheses.18 Careful deltoid
reconstruction is necessary if the insertion is compromised with resection. Synthetic
grafts can be used to help rebuild a capsular check rein19 (Figure 9).

Humeral diaphysis
Lesions in the humeral diaphysis and metadiaphysis generally can be managed via
internal fixation with the use of an intramedullary nail or plate/screw construct.
Both methods are effective. Ultimately, implant selection depends on surgeon preference.
Internal fixation
Indicated in patients without segmental bone loss
Treatment options include anterolateral plating and antegrade intramedullary nailing.20
Intramedullary nailing (Figure 10)

If adjunct radiation therapy is considered (eg, in patients with multiple myeloma and
metastatic lung cancer), antegrade intramedullary nailing should be considered to
protect the irradiated bone from pathologic fracture.
Perioperative radiation therapy for these lesions may afford longer-lasting symptom
relief and serve as an important adjunct treatment option.
Intramedullary nailing can be performed via an open or closed antegrade approach.
Proximal and distal locking generally are recommended to ensure rigid fixation,
especially in patients with a pathologic fracture.
Overall advantages include low risk of implant failure, ability to protect a long
segment of diseased bone, and insertion via a minimally invasive approach that
minimizes soft-tissue injury and decreases the potential for wound healing
complications because of smaller incisions.
Disadvantages include mandatory entry through the rotator cuff, requiring
subsequent repair with intramedullary non-nail fixation.

balloon that is placed over a guidewire. The balloon is filled with a monomer liquid,
which is then cured with a light source, offering rigid fixation (Figure 11).
Can be used as a stand-alone technique in patients with limited prognosis
Can be used to supplement plate fixation (Figure 11)

These lesions are better addressed via curettage and plate fixation, with adjunct
PMMA packing to help decrease metastatic burden.
A major advantage of plate fixation is that the rotator cuff is not disturbed.
Major disadvantages include increased blood loss, potential for nerve injury, and
inability to span the entire length of the humerus.
Intercalary resection with reconstruction (Figure 12)
Large and destructive lesions of the humeral diaphysis with segmental bone loss
Can be managed via resection of the affected segment and reconstruction with the
use of a modular intercalary endoprosthesis or an intercalary structural allograft
Intercalary endoprosthetic reconstruction allows for immediate–weight bearing and
immediate use of the arm without the need for bony healing. Torsional forces are
the primary cause of complications, such as aseptic loosening.21,22
• Allograft can used as an alternative intercalary construct; however, it may be
associated with delayed union and nonunion at graft-host junction sites.16 This is not
a pragmatic solution for patients who display limited prognosis, active disease,
surgical treatment without the goal of curative intent, or in a radiated field.

Distal humerus
Distal humerus metastatic lesions generally are symptomatic.
This is partially because the supracondylar region of the humerus creates a natural
stress riser.
Metastatic lesions with cortical compromise usually generate considerable pain.
Flexible nails
Flexible, crossed nails inserted at the elbow may be considered and may protect
the entire humerus.
PMMA cement packing also should be considered.
Overall, this construct affords less stability and rotational control than other
internal fixation methods, including plating.
Plating (Figure 13)
Generally used to restore the integrity of the columns of the distal humerus
Dual orthogonal constructs can add stability.
PMMA augmentation is a useful adjunct and may result in a durable construct for
pain relief and preservation of elbow function.
Periarticular bone stock must remain to allow for adequate fixation.
Usually, an extensile triceps splitting posterior approach can be used. The radial
nerve generally is identified 12 to 16 cm proximal from the lateral epicondyle.

Forearm, wrist, and hand
Metastatic disease of the forearm, wrist, and hand is uncommon..
Lung and renal metastases have the highest predilection to present distal to the
elbow.
Internal fixation with the use of plates, screws, and wires remains the standard
treatment option if mechanical stability is compromised.
At the proximal ulna and he distal radius, restoration of articular congruity is critical
and can be achieved with use of PMMA cement packing alone or in combination
with internal fixation (Figure 14).

diagnosis of metastatic gastrointestinal carcinoma. A, Preoperative radiograph
demonstrates an atraumatic pathologic radius fracture. B, Radiograph obtained
after open reduction and internal fixation, cementation, and adjuvant radiation
therapy. (Courtesy of Drew D. Moore, MD, Royal Oak, MI.)
At the proximal radius and the distal ulna, PMMA cement packing remains the
preferred treatment option.

If extensive disease that may not be amenable to packing alone is present in
these regions, resection may be considered.
Resection of the proximal radius and the distal ulna generally results in minimal
postoperative morbidity or functional loss because the interosseous membrane
remains intact and limits migration.
In the hand, small, destructive lesions generally are managed via curettage and
PMMA cement packing alone (Figure 15).
In larger bones of the hand (ie, metacarpals or phalanges), internal fixation with
the use of smooth Kirschner wires or small plates also may be considered.
If a tumor is extensively destructive of the bone and soft tissues, an ablative
procedure, such as a ray amputation, may be considered.

Surgical Approaches
The general approach to proximal humerus lesions involves appreciation of the size of
the lesion and its extension into and destruction of the articular surface. These factors

9/4/26, 9:44 AM
AAOS | Surgical Management of Upper Extremity Bone Metastases
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000566
20/30

can help determine whether the patient will benefit from plate stabilization or require
arthroplasty. If the lesion remains well contained within the metaphysis, with sufficient
epiphyseal bone stock to allow for screw purchase, and no evidence of articular surface
destruction is observed, then plate fixation can be pursued with the use of a proximal
humerus locking plate with or without PMMA cement.8,16 Ideally, with this approach, the
native greater and lesser tuberosities are preserved along with their soft-tissue
attachments to maintain shoulder function, if possible.8 The use of locking plates may
confer improved biomechanical stability over nonlocking plates and intramedullary
devices.8,16 In addition, PMMA cement augmentation can be used to fill bone defects,
thereby conferring immediate stability, especially in tumor histologies that are less
prone to healing.9,10 Siegel et al16 assessed the role of locked plating and PMMA cement
in the management of 32 pathologic proximal humerus fractures. The authors reported
no hardware failure (over a mean follow-up of 17.6 months) and that all of the patients
returned to their previous occupation without restrictions at a mean follow-up of
approximately 6 weeks.16
In large, uncontained lesions of the proximal humerus involving the glenohumeral
articulation, proximal humerus arthroplasty is preferred, specifically a humeral
hemiarthroplasty implant.23,24 These implants generally offer adequate shoulder
function with low complication rates; however, the functional results of patients who
undergo hemiarthroplasty depend on the degree of remaining rotator cuff and the
potential for the greater and lesser tuberosities to heal and maintain the rotator cuff
soft-tissue attachments. Soft-tissue failure in these patients can cause debilitating pain
and result in anterosuperior escape, which portends poor shoulder function.24
Therefore, reverse TSA has increased in popularity. Many studies have demonstrated
improved shoulder function and pain control with reverse TSA implants in patients
undergoing oncologic reconstructions.17,24-30 Despite the advantages of reverse TSA,
hemiarthroplasty still maintains a role, especially as a palliative procedure in older,
lower-demand patients.
Pathologic lesions in the humeral diaphysis can be managed with the use of an
intramedullary nail or a plate and screw construct. Although both options are effective,
specific advantages and disadvantages are associated with each construct.3,4,8,31 In a
review of more than 300 humeral metastases–related procedures, no difference was

found between intramedullary nailing and plate and screw fixation with regard to the
incidence of revision surgery, systemic complications, surgical time, and hospital length
of stay.32 The only differences noted between the two procedures was the mean
estimated blood loss, which was higher in the plate fixation group compared with the
intramedullary nailing group (472 mL versus 165 mL).32 The intramedullary nail offers
some biomechanical advantages, including its ability to load share and easily span
almost the entire humerus. A nail also can be inserted via smaller surgical incisions. The
latter may minimize intraoperative blood loss, pain, and wound healing complications.32
The main disadvantage of an antegrade intramedullary humeral nail is its potential for
shoulder pain and rotator cuff tendon irritation.3,4 Plate and screw fixation is associated
with advantages if the surgeon is already planning to perform an open procedure for
curettage of the lesion or if a lesion that extends from the diaphysis into the metaphysis
and epiphysis cannot be effectively spanned with the use of an intramedullary nail.2-
4,8,31 In addition, a plate and screw construct may avoid the rotator cuff insertion,
allowing for direct reduction of the pathologic fracture and minimizing spread of tumor
because the intramedullary canal is not sounded with reamers and guidewires. The main
disadvantages of plate fixation include larger incisions, increased blood loss, potentially
increased risk for infection, and inability to protect the entire humerus. Intercalary
resection with reconstruction is a third option to manage humeral diaphyseal metastatic
lesions. This procedure primarily is reserved for patients with a large, destructive lesion
of the humeral diaphysis and segmental bone loss. In a multicenter review of 44
intercalary implants, Benevenia et al33 reported five failures (11%) because of aseptic
loosening (between the stem and bone) and six structural failures (14%) occurring at the
clamp-rod implant interface. A deep infection occurred in one patient, and tumor
progression that required amputation occurred in another patient.
Only 7% of humeral metastatic lesions occur in the distal humerus.15 Although the
treatment algorithm for these lesions is similar to that for proximal humerus lesions, the
unique anatomy of the distal humerus combined with its close proximity to
neurovascular structures, a short articular segment, and the modest soft-tissue envelope
contribute to the challenge in managing metastatic lesions in this region. Most lesions in
the distal humerus can be managed with the use of single- or dual-column distal
humerus locking plates.1-4,15,31 Lesions that are large and uncontained and involve the
articular surface or extend into the elbow joint can be managed via resection of the

technically challenging and are associated with a high complication rate (18% to 45%
revision rate, with aseptic humeral stem loosening and infection being the most
common reasons of failure), including lifelong activity restrictions and limitations in
elbow function.34-36
Metastatic lesions distal to the elbow are rare and comprise less than 0.1% of all cases in
the upper extremity.37,38 These lesions usually are observed in patients with metastatic
lung or renal cancer, with their presence typically indicating advanced disease. Given
their rarity, no standardized treatment protocol exists; however, nonsurgical treatment
options are commonly used to aid in palliation. In the forearm, most lesions can be
managed via systemic therapy and external beam radiation therapy, with potential
stabilization with the use of a splint or cast. Proximal and diaphyseal ulnar lesions and
distal and diaphyseal radial lesions that remain painful despite nonsurgical management
can be managed via curettage, PMMA cementation, and plate and screw fixation or
flexible nails.1-3 Similarly, lesions in the proximal radius or the distal ulna in which
nonsurgical management fails can be managed via surgical resection.37,38
Postoperative Management
Adjunct treatment options
Radiation therapy
Postoperative radiation therapy often is used as an adjunct to surgical fixation to improve
local tumor control.
Radiation therapy may decrease the risk for continued bone destruction, implant
loosening/loss of fixation, and the need for additional surgical management.39
Postoperative radiation therapy generally is delayed 10 to 14 days postoperatively to allow
the surgical incision adequate time to heal.
Systemic therapy
Systemic management via chemotherapy and/or immunotherapy is critical in the overall
treatment patients with metastatic disease.
However, these agents may cause substantial adverse events postoperatively, including
wound healing complications. Therefore, appropriate treatment holidays must be

while limiting interruptions in systemic therapy and overall oncologic care.
Diphosphonates or denosumab should be added to the systemic treatment regimen to
prevent additional skeletal-related events.
Postoperative management
A main goal of surgical management of metastatic disease is to restore immediate function
of the surgical extremity.
Patients may begin range of motion at the elbow and shoulder during the first postoperative
week.
Sutures/staples generally can be removed 2 to 3 weeks postoperatively; however, certain
situations, such as preoperative radiation therapy and concomitant administration of
immunotherapy, may necessitate leaving sutures/staples in place for a longer period.

In a large study of 295 consecutive patients who underwent surgical treatment for an
impending or pathologic humerus fracture, Janssen et al32 reported an 8.5% revision
surgery rate, with the primary reasons for revision surgery being deep infection (2%),
nonunion (2%), peri-implant fracture (1.4%), allograft nonunion (1%), massive hematoma
(0.68%), tumor progression (0.68%), compartment syndrome (0.34%), and early plate
loosening in an intercalary allograft construct (0.34%). In the same study, a stratified
analysis based on surgery/implant type revealed a revision surgery rate of 11% in
patients who underwent endoprosthetic reconstruction, 10% in patients who underwent
plate and screw fixation, and 6.7% in patients who underwent humeral intramedullary
nailing.32 Similarly, 5.8% of patients in this cohort had systemic postoperative
complications, including pneumonia (3.7%), sepsis (0.68%), and fat embolism (0.34%).32
Although the overall incidence of complications after the surgical management of upper
extremity metastatic bone lesions is rare, the approach to managing these complications
is important. Certain complications, such as tumor progression, require involvement of
the multidisciplinary oncologic treatment team, including the medical oncologist, to
determine the most appropriate next steps, including resumption of
chemotherapy/immunotherapy and/or involvement of palliative care services, including
palliative external beam radiation treatment.
Outcomes
Pain relief is reliably noted in more than 90% of patients treated via rigid fixation.40-42
Functional range of motion and recovery of the arm for activities of daily living also is observed
in most patients after surgical treatment via rigid internal fixation.43
Most treatment failures are secondary to disease progression or early loss of fixation.39
Patients with renal cell carcinoma are especially prone to disease progression and often are
treated via higher doses of adjuvant radiation therapy or more aggressive surgical excision to
decrease the risk for early failure.
